content.intro: Learn referential actions through a short explanation, a concept diagram, and a PostgreSQL-oriented example. Focus on the reason for the query or design decision before memorizing syntax.
content.why_it_matters: Referential Actions matters because database behavior becomes more reliable when the intended row meaning, data shape, and edge cases are explicit. This lesson follows the SQL curriculum's listed subtopics and calls out PostgreSQL-specific behavior when it matters.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Use referential actions to make database structure and data rules explicit. Preview changes, name constraints deliberately, consider dependencies, and keep schema evolution in versioned, reviewable scripts.

content_blocks.title: Apply the idea
content_blocks.text: Start with the subtopics: ON DELETE CASCADE, ON DELETE SET NULL, ON DELETE RESTRICT and related behavior, ON UPDATE behavior where supported. Define the result you expect, run or inspect the small example in your own disposable PostgreSQL lab, and change one assumption at a time. The embedded lesson editor is a demonstration shell: the current project shows the sample expected output and does not execute arbitrary SQL on the server.

items.title: ON DELETE CASCADE
items.text: ON DELETE CASCADE changes stored data. Preview the target rows, specify a restrictive predicate where appropriate, validate constraints, and wrap related changes in a transaction that can be reviewed before commit.

items.title: ON DELETE SET NULL
items.text: ON DELETE SET NULL requires deliberate handling of absent or unknown values. In SQL, NULL is not the same as zero or an empty string; use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL for direct tests and check how expressions and aggregates propagate unknowns.

items.title: ON DELETE RESTRICT and related behavior
items.text: ON DELETE RESTRICT and related behavior changes stored data. Preview the target rows, specify a restrictive predicate where appropriate, validate constraints, and wrap related changes in a transaction that can be reviewed before commit.

items.title: Choosing referential actions safely
items.text: Choosing referential actions safely helps you translate business rules into keys, constraints, normalized schemas, and migration plans that keep invalid data out of the database. Start with a concrete example, state the expected result, and verify the behavior before extending the query or design.

content_blocks.code:
CREATE TEMP TABLE parent_demo (parent_id integer PRIMARY KEY);
CREATE TEMP TABLE child_demo (child_id integer PRIMARY KEY, parent_id integer REFERENCES parent_demo(parent_id) ON DELETE SET NULL);
content_blocks.expected_output: The foreign key defines a deletion action for dependent rows. Choose CASCADE, SET NULL, RESTRICT, or NO ACTION only when it matches the business rule.

The CodeLeaf lesson Run button in this scaffold only previews the documented expected output; it is not a SQL execution service.
content_blocks.reset_steps: For queries, restore the original text and compare results. For statements that change data, use the transaction and rollback shown in the example, or recreate the disposable lab from the included setup instructions. Do not reset production data.

content_blocks.title: Remember
content_blocks.text: SQL correctness depends on data shape, constraints, NULL behavior, row counts, and the target database dialect—not just whether a statement parses.

task_acceptance_criteria: The query or design example matches the lesson's intended behavior.
The expected row grain and relevant NULL, duplicate, boundary, or permission behavior are explained.
The test is performed only in the local disposable lab, or clearly marked as a static inspection when a real runner is unavailable.
hints: Begin with the subtopic on delete cascade and write down the result you expect.
Use the smallest valid example; verify table and column names before adding complexity.
Inspect one edge case: missing values, duplicate matches, tied sort values, a constraint violation, or an engine-specific syntax difference.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a query is correct because it returns some rows.
common_mistakes.why: A result can omit valid records, multiply joined rows, mishandle NULLs, or rely on a non-deterministic order.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected row grain, add targeted edge cases, and use a stable tie-breaker whenever order or pagination matters.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying PostgreSQL syntax into another SQL engine without checking support.
common_mistakes.why: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, and Oracle differ in types, functions, row limits, procedural features, and transaction behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Label the target engine/version and verify the relevant official reference before adapting the query.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing with production data or credentials.
common_mistakes.why: Practice statements can change rows or expose sensitive information if run against the wrong connection.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a dedicated disposable lab, check current_database() and current_user, and review all changes before committing.
